## DwarfStar 4 Introduces Specialized Asymmetric Quantization for Local Frontier Inference

DwarfStar has released DwarfStar 4 (ds4), a specialized C-based inference engine designed to run large-scale frontier open-weight models on high-memory hardware, according to the official project site. The engine is optimized for Apple Silicon (Metal), NVIDIA (CUDA), and AMD (ROCm) architectures, enabling the local execution of massive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that typically require remote cloud serving.

The development addresses the technical challenge of running high-parameter models on consumer or workstation-grade hardware by utilizing "asymmetric quantization." This approach targets routed experts for heavy compression while maintaining precision in critical shared paths, allowing complex models to fit within limited VRAM/RAM footprints without significant loss of intelligence.

signals.excerpt:
As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services.

The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot, and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models, Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios.

Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.
...
That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure.

Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden.
...
As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale.
...
Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures.

Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM.

Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt.

Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope.

Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments.

Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. That density allows Microsoft to serve more simultaneous AI interactions and larger workloads from each rack, improving datacenter capacity and the economics of expanding AI services.

Maia 300 will begin production deployments in 2027. For more information on Maia 300 architectural details, read our technical paper.

Samsung's sub-1-bit quantization paper gets a reality check, plus fresh research on tiny LLMs and ESP32 voice silicon.

Samsung Research's NanoQuant, a post-training quantization method accepted at ICML 2026, compresses a Llama2-70B model from 138GB down to 5.35GB — a 25.8x reduction done in 13 hours on a single H100. The resulting model then runs on a consumer 8GB RTX 3050 at up to 20.11 tokens per second, according to the paper's own benchmark table.

That part is genuine. What spread online this week inflated it further: the paper is actually eight months old, its runtime table shows a 13B model needing 1.70GB (not the tinier figures quoted in viral posts), and the social retelling dropped two real costs — measurable quality loss at these bit rates and custom CUDA kernels that only work on NVIDIA hardware. A write-up by singularity.kiwi traced the numbers back to the source and flagged the gap.

For edge devices the honest takeaway is narrower than the headline: sub-1-bit quantization can put a 70B-class model on a single consumer GPU, but only with vendor-specific kernels and a quality tax nobody has fully quantified outside the paper itself.
...

Self-reported results: at 6 bits, STEPQuant matches FP32-state accuracy on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B; at 4 bits it beats uniform INT8. In SGLang with custom kernels, the authors claim over 5x state compression and up to 68.7% less total serving memory.

signals.title: ReplaySSM: Rethinking State Storage for Faster Hybrid-Model Decoding | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Building on earlier ReplaySSM work, NVIDIA and the Dao AI Lab at Princeton University explore how caching SSM inputs speeds up decoding and supports low-precision state with less error accumulation.
...
* ReplaySSM represents state-space model state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, separating output computation from state updates.
* The technique reduces state memory traffic by roughly half, speeding up SSM decoding kernels by 1.46x to 1.80x at batch size 256 on NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs.
* ReplaySSM simplifies speculative decoding rollback by appending draft inputs to a buffer instead of snapshotting state, delivering 1.85x to 2.10x higher speculative throughput on 120B-class models.
* Using a high-precision checkpoint for recurrence and a low-precision copy for reads limits quantization error accumulation, keeping three of four evaluated models within about 2 percentage points of FP32 accuracy on GPQA-Diamond.
...
SSM layers are designed to make decoding fast: they use a fixed-size state in place of a key-value (KV) cache that grows with context length. At serving batch sizes, however, the SSM layers, not attention, can be the latency bottleneck up to 100K tokens of context. SSM layers also complicate two techniques that reliably speed up attention decoding: speculative decoding and quantization.
ReplaySSM makes SSM layers the fast part again. It represents the SSM state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs. Perplexity released pplx-embed-v2-late on 7 October: two open-weight retrieval models, at 0.6B and 9B parameters, published on Hugging Face under an MIT licence. They are late-interaction retrievers in the ColBERT mould, emitting a 128-dimensional vector for every token rather than compressing a document into one vector, and scoring a query against a document with MaxSim — each query token picks its best-matching document token, and those maxima are summed.

signals.excerpt:
Mistral has unveiled Mistral Large 4 (commonly nicknamed "Le Chonk"), a 1.05-trillion-parameter multimodal model launching first as a public preview API ahead of an anticipated open-weight release.

What happened: The French AI lab released ML4 to developers via Mistral Studio and OpenRouter, offering a 1-million token context window, a 256,144 token maximum output limit, and native tool calling. The API is live now; the model weights are scheduled for release later this month to allow the market to benchmark performance across security, finance, and software engineering tasks.
...
Mistral Large 4 represents a maturation in how frontier open-weight models are scaled and distributed. Architecturally, ML4 operates as a granular Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) system with a total of 1.05 trillion parameters, a 1.6-billion-parameter vision encoder, and 52 billion active parameters per token. Some early third-party coverage mistakenly reported 49B active parameters, highlighting the friction that occurs when complex MoE specifications hit fast-moving news cycles.
...
ML4's most transformative technical specifications are its input and output limits. The model provides a 1-million token context window paired with a 256,144 maximum output limit. For AI infrastructure, that changes the paradigm: a 256K output limit shifts models from merely reading vast amounts of data to generating massive artifacts in a single shot—rewriting entire codebases, drafting comprehensive legal treatises, or exporting structured enterprise knowledge bases without hitting generation caps.

Mistral's rollout strategy is deliberate. Rather than releasing weights on the open internet immediately, the company launched a "public preview" through Mistral Studio and partners like OpenRouter. This API-first, staggered release both generates immediate commercial revenue and lets developers benchmark latency, pricing, and caching economics while maintaining appetite for the forthcoming open-weight drop. The approach also tempers early open-source deployment chaos by routing initial usage through managed environments.

The model is optimized for what Mistral terms "agentic workloads." Standard generalized benchmarks are being deprioritized in favor of workflow-centric evaluations: ML4 is being tuned and assessed on targeted suites such as DeepSWE v1.1, Terminal-Bench 4, and the Coding Agent Index. The positioning is explicit: ML4 is intended as an autonomous coding engine capable of executing terminal commands, calling external tools, and enforcing structured outputs, not just a conversational chatbot.

Mistral also addressed enterprise adoption friction. Behind the "Le Chonk" branding, the company published rigorous downstream-provider technical documentation—provider identification, publication dates, and general-purpose AI classification status—before weights were released. That paper trail helps compliance and legal teams evaluate private-cloud or on-prem deployments and signals that open-weight AI is moving from developer playgrounds toward governed enterprise infrastructure.
...
This independent, research-based analysis synthesizes official API specifications, technical governance documentation, and developer market benchmarks to provide a clear-eyed view of Mistral Large 4. It is written for CTOs, AI strategists, and platform engineers evaluating next-generation frontier AI infrastructure and open-weight deployment models.
...
The ML4 launch shows that the frontier of open-weight AI is no longer solely about matching proprietary benchmarks; it's about mastering distribution and governance. By throttling the open-weight release behind a preview API and packaging the launch with compliance documentation, Mistral is converting models into calculated commercial offerings aimed at enterprise on-prem budgets.

# SGLang and Miles on NVIDIA Vera Rubin

# SGLang and Miles
...
We had early access to two NVIDIA Vera Rubin nodes (8 GPUs) and used them to bring SGLang and Miles up on the platform: SGLang for inference and Miles for RL training. On the inference side, we tuned SGLang for Kimi K3 NVFP4: this post covers what we changed in the attention, MoE/communication and KDA kernels, and how much each change bought. On the training side, Miles, which uses SGLang for rollout and Megatron for training, runs RL end to end on Vera Rubin out of the box, including agentic RL with sandboxes on the Vera CPU.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin is the GPU generation after NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (GB300 NVL72). For kernel work, the most impactful changes are more shared memory per CTA (327 KiB, up from the 227 KiB on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell), more SMs (212 on our nodes), and NVIDIA NVLink 6. Some of our changes retune Blackwell-era kernels for these new limits. The rest remove overheads we found while profiling Kimi K3 on Rubin, such as kernel launches, barrier stalls and hidden copies.

Cognition has deployed Vera Rubin NVL72 with its own SGLang-based stack and has reported up to a 4.8x increase in total token throughput over GB200 NVL72. 1

## Inference: Serving Kimi K3 NVFP4

Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter hybrid model with a 1M-token context window. Its 93 attention layers interleave 69 KDA linear-attention layers with 24 MLA layers, and every attention output is banked and aggregated per block through Attention Residuals. The FFN is a LatentMoE with 896 experts, top-16 routing, running in a 3584-dimensional latent space. We serve the NVFP4 checkpoint with RadixArk's DSpark block speculative decoding, so every decode step is a short draft pass followed by a verify pass over the drafted tokens.
...
eeper MLA pipelines. In long context settings, MLA decode spends most of its time waiting on KV reads from HBM, and the way to hide that is to keep more reads in flight. On Blackwell, the FP8 kernel had already filled its 227 KiB of shared memory with 3 K stages and 2 V stages. Vera Rubin raises the per-CTA limit to 327 KiB, just enough for a fourth K stage and two more V stages. With the deeper pipeline, MLA at batch 16 and 128k context runs 16% faster, with bit-identical output.
...
Fused MoE tail. Every MoE layer ends the same way: finalize the expert outputs, add the shared expert, all-reduce across 8 GPUs, then RMSNorm. Each of those kernels is tiny, so launch overhead dominates, and K3 pays it in all 92 MoE layers. We defer the finalization and fold all four steps into one collective kernel. That removes 276 launches per decode step and gives 5.9% end to end.
...
higher concurrency. The fused tail ... all-reduce ... ones. On
...
Less stall in KDA verify. KDA's fused verify kernel spent much of its time waiting at barriers instead of computing. Every CTA copied its conv weights into shared memory and then waited at a block-wide barrier. Now each warp keeps its own weights in registers. State handoffs that stay inside one warp require no CTA barriers. The v warps finish precomputing early, so they now use that idle time to compute the output-norm gate. Outputs stay bitwise identical. On Vera Rubin, the production verify kernel sped up by 20%.
...
Strided output gate. The gated RMSNorm in each KDA layer takes its gate from a column slice of the fused QKVG projection. Because the slice isn't contiguous, PyTorch silently copied it before every call: 2.6 µs, 69 times per step. Teaching the norm kernel to read ... gate through its strides removed the copy and cut decode step time ... 1.8
...
## RL training: Miles on NVIDIA Vera Rubin

Miles runs RL training end to end on NVIDIA Vera Rubin, with SGLang for rollout and Megatron for training, from a single container image. With the Rubin-enablement PR in place, these RL runs were launched out of the box using Miles, on a single tray (4 GPUs):

- Qwen3-30B-A3B on GSM8K (256 prompts × 8 samples per rollout, up to 1,024 response tokens): training converges as expected, with reward rising from about 45% to 95% over 50 rollouts (Figure ... ), which matches the GB30 ... reward growth curve perfectly.
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash (4-layer, FP8) on GSM8K (32 prompts × 8 samples per step, up to 256 response tokens): the FP8 path runs end-to-end for both rollout and training.
...
These are promising initial results demonstrating Miles' readiness on Vera Rubin. The next phase will focus on scaling up and further improving performance.
...
As a first step toward agentic RL on Vera Rubin, we run it on a single tray with NeMo Gym's mini-SWE-agent environment: each episode gets its own sandbox on the tray's Vera CPU, next to the GPUs that serve and train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, with 64 sandboxes running at once. We chose SWE-bench Verified because it ships prebuilt arm64 task images, and we verified that grading works on them. Each step samples 8 tasks × 8 attempts from a 64-task pool, with up to 64K tokens per episode. Training runs normally with all environments on the Arm-based Vera CPU: the reward holds at about 0.6, episodes get about 30% shorter, and rollout and training stay closely matched (Figure 4). Once Vera CPU servers are available at scale, we look forward to agentic training with far more concurrent environments.
...

On inference, we'll keep rolling out optimizations to take full advantage of the platform across a wider range of production workloads. On training, Miles will focus on scaling up and improving performance, and on agentic RL with far more concurrent environments once Vera CPU servers are available at scale.

```
Gemma 4 E2B in Pure JAX on a Colab TPU: Google's 4-Bit Export Against an Exact Repack — Web Pulse

 [ARTICLE · art-148562] src= dev.to ↗ pub= 2026-10 ... 10T00:51Z topic= large-language-models verified= true sentiment=↑ positive 

# Gemma 4 E2B in Pure JAX on a Colab TPU: Google's 4-Bit Export Against an Exact Repack

A developer published an Apache 2.0 Colab notebook that serves Gemma 4 E2B on a single TPU v5e chip using a pure-JAX engine and compares Google's 4-bit QAT export against an exact repack of the trained quantization grid. The repack lands 342.6 times closer to the original model in next-token predictions, matches its top token 99.29% of the time versus 85.96%, and downloads 0.8 GB less because Google's export redundantly stores lm_head.weight as a copy of the token embedding.
...
This article provides a step by step guide to a Colab notebook that serves Gemma 4 E2B on a single TPU v5e chip with a pure-JAX engine and compares two 4-bit builds of the same model against the weights Google trained. Every number below was measured in the notebook on a Colab v5e-1 runtime, and the executed notebook is committed.

Google ships E2B in 4 bits as `gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-w4a16-ct`. Its export rounds every weight a second time, onto a grid the model never trained on. A repack that stores the trained grid instead lands 342.6 times closer to the original model in next-token predictions, matches its top token 99.29% of the time against 85.96%, writes the same 128-token story word for word, runs at the same speed and downloads 0.8 GB less.

This notebook is an entry in the AI GDE Marathon: JAX on TPU Tutorial, a series of Apache 2.0 Colab notebooks covering JAX on the TPU backend. Colab's TPU runtimes are the same v5e and v6e silicon the source measurements came from, so every cell measures on the reader's chip and prints the source result beside it as context.

Gemma 4 E2B was trained with quantization-aware training (QAT): during training every weight was held on a 4-bit grid, one scale per group of 32 values, so the model learned to work with exactly those values. Google publishes the result twice:

| Build | Hugging Face | What it stores |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QAT reference | `google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized` | the trained grid values, in bf16 |
| Google's export | `google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-w4a16-ct` | int4, each group re-rounded with step = largest weight ÷ 7.5 |
| The repack | `xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct` | int4, the trained levels and the trained step |

Both 4-bit builds use the same compressed-tensors W4A16 format and the same shapes, so any that reads one reads the other. The difference is which numbers are inside.
...
Cell 1.2 clones the engine, `tpu-jax`, at a pinned commit. It is a Gemma 4 E2B decoder in pure JAX with no PyTorch in the path, and its 4-bit path unpacks each weight with plain XLA operations before multiplying.
...
```
qat      1951 tensors     0 packed int4   lm_head stored: False
stock    2504 tensors   276 packed int4   lm_head stored: True
repack   2503 tensors   276 packed int4   lm_head stored: False

stock lm_head identical to embed_tokens: True   (0.805 GB)
stock minus repack on disk: 0.805 GB
...
Both 4-bit builds pack the same 276 linear layers. Google's export also stores `lm_head.weight`, a byte-for-byte copy of the token embedding, although the config ties the two. That one tensor is the whole 0.8 GB difference in download size.
...
Google's export uses largest weight ÷ 7.5 as the step in every group, and its values sit 6.7% from the trained ones. The repack sits 0.19% away, three values in four are bit-for-bit the trained value, and the rest differ only by the bf16 rounding of the stored step.
...
Cells 4.2 to 4.4 load each model in turn, feed all three the same 8 WikiText-2 sequences of 512 tokens, and keep each model's predicted next-token distribution at every position. Cell 4.5 compares each 4-bit build with the QAT model on the same 4,096 positions:

```
build     mean KL  same top token  perplexity ratio   per-sequence mean KL, min to max
stock     0.07141          85.96%            1.0643   0.05807 to 0.08348
repack    0.00021          99.29%            0.9994   0.00015 to 0.00028

positions where the repack is closer to the QAT model than the stock build: 100.0% of 4,096
stock KL / repack KL: 342.6x

```

The repack is closer to the QAT model at every one of the 4,096 positions, and the gap holds on every sequence: the stock build's best sequence is still 200 times further off than the repack's worst. Google's export also predicts the text 6.4% worse than the model it was made from.
...
The two 4-bit builds tie on speed and put the same 6.56 GB on the chip, because the engine never loads the duplicate `lm_head`. The repack writes the QAT model's story token for token. Google's export opens with the same five words, " is a vast and complex", then writes "narrative" where the QAT model writes "tapestry", and the two stories diverge from there.

The bf16 QAT model decodes faster than either 4-bit build in this engine, because the engine unpacks every 4-bit weight at every step. The engine can unpack once at load instead (`dequant_at_load=True`), which trades the HBM saving for that speed.
...
The absolute speeds differ between the pairs because the engines differ: vLLM's int4 kernel against a reference unpack-then-multiply in pure JAX. The ratio inside each pair is what carries, and it is 0.999x under vLLM and 0.996x here. The same holds for quality: under vLLM on a 3,880-record test suite the repack scored 67.8% against 65.5%, 2.4 points higher (95% range +1.4 to +3.4) and within 0.6 points of the bf16 release.

| | Google's export | The repack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Error against the trained weights | 🔴 6.7% | 🟢 0.19% |
| Mean KL against the QAT model | 🔴 0.07141 | 🟢 0.00021 |
| Same top token as the QAT model | 85.96% | 🟢 99.29% |
| Greedy story tokens equal to QAT | 🔴 5 of 128 | 🟢 128 of 128 |
| Download | 8.32 GB | 🟢 7.51 GB |
| Weights on the chip | 6.56 GB | 6.56 GB |
| Decode tok/s, one request | 93.7 | 93.3 |
| Format | compressed-tensors W4A16 | compressed-tensors W4A16 |

The repack. It holds the weights Google trained, runs at the same speed in the same format, puts the same bytes on the chip and is 0.8 GB smaller to download. Any that reads Google's `-qat-w4a16-ct` reads it unchanged, so switching is a change of repo name.

The goal of this notebook was to measure, on a reader's own Colab TPU, whether Google's 4-bit Gemma 4 E2B export holds the weights the model was trained on, and what a repack that holds them exactly changes. The key to the solution was putting all three checkpoints through one pure-JAX , one forward pass, one text and one prompt, with the QAT checkpoint as the reference for both 4-bit builds. The results were:

Scope: one Colab v5e-1 runtime (one TPU v5 lite chip, 16.91 GB HBM), JAX 0.7.2, `tpu-jax` at commit `4b9f8e9`, run on 2026-10-09. The output comparison uses 8 WikiText-2 test sequences of 512 tokens, and speed is the median of three 128-token greedy runs of one prompt. The 3,880-record test suite and the vLLM speeds are earlier results on a v5e chip, cited as context. The repack is unofficial and derived from Google's release under Apache 2.0. Parts of the analysis and writing were done with AI assistance (Claude); every figure comes from the committed executed notebook.

The comparison of Google's 4-bit Gemma 4 E2B export against an exact repack was validated on a Colab TPU with an incremental step by step approach.

# ReasonRAG：仅用5k数据超越90k训练的SOTA模型，大模型RAG训练新范式 

 张小明 

 前端开发工程师 

 ReasonRAG：仅用5k数据超越90k训练 ... SOTA模型，大模型RAG训练新范式 

ReasonRAG是由港城大与华为诺亚方舟实验室提出的基于过程监督的Agentic RAG训练框架，通过SPRE设计过程级奖励，结合MCTS探索高质量推理路径，构建了首个过程监督数据集RAG-ProGuide。该方法仅需5k训练数据就在多个评测集上超越了需90k数据的SOTA模型，显著提升了数据效率、多跳推理能力和跨领域泛化性能，为复杂推理任务提供了更细粒度、更稳定的优化信号。相关代码与数据已开源。

今天为大家分享来自香港城市大学与华为诺亚方舟实验室的最新工作 ReasonRAG。该工作提出一种过程监督的 Agentic RAG训练框架，通过为模型推理的每一步提供细粒度的“过程奖励”，显著提升了复杂推理任务的性能与效率。作者还为此构建了首个过程监督偏好数据集 RAG-ProGuide。该方法仅用 5k 数据就在多个权威评测集上超越了需 90k 数据训练的 SOTA 模型，展现出极高的数据效率。相关代码与数据已开源。
...
为突破这一限制，“Agentic RAG”应运而生——它让模型能够自主决策是否检索、生成查询、抽取证据、合成答案，在复杂推理中表现出更强的灵活性。近期如Search-R1等方法将强化学习引入Agentic RAG训练流程，通过最终答案的正确与否作为唯一奖励信号，取得了一定进展。
...
为此，团队首次将过程监督强化学习方法系统性引入Agentic RAG训练流程，构建出全新框架——ReasonRAG。该方法通过细粒度奖励机制、基于搜索的路径构建和偏好优化训练策略，显著提升了模型在多跳问答、多轮推理场景下的能力。在多个权威评测集上，ReasonRAG在仅使用5k训练数据的情况下，就超越了使用90k数据训练的Search-R1。
...
ReasonRAG 由五个核心组件构成，形成了从数据自动生成到策略训练、推理部署的闭环体系：
...
- 使用**Shortest Path Reward Estimation（SPRE）**设计过程级奖励；
- 借助MCTS搜索算法在Agentic推理空间中探索高质量中间步骤；
- 自动生成过程偏好数据集RAG-ProGuide；
- 基于该数据集进行偏好策略优化（DPO）；
- 模型在推理时根据任务复杂度动态决定检索与回答流程。
...
传统的强化学习中，reward通常只针对最终结果。但在Agentic RAG中，每一步推理决策（如生成查询或提取证据）都会影响整体推理质量。因此，ReasonRAG提出Shortest Path Reward Estimation（SPRE），为每一步决策分配一个过程奖励。

该方法会对当前推理路径进行多次模拟（Monte Carlo rollout），模拟完整推理过程，并评估其最终正确性与路径长度。SPRE通过惩罚冗长路径，引导模型学会以更短、更精准的方式完成任务，从而实现效率与准确性兼顾的学习目标。这种奖励机制为训练过程提供了高频、结构化、动态的反馈信号。
...
为了从海量可能的推理路径中找到优质策略，ReasonRAG引入了经典的 Monte Carlo Tree Search（MCTS），将整个Agentic RAG推理过程形式化为状态-动作树（state-action tree），并在该树上进行探索。
...
基于SPRE和MCTS，作者构建了首个专为过程级奖励设计的Agentic RAG数据集：RAG-ProGuide。

该数据集从三个常见QA数据集中（PopQA、HotpotQA、2WikiMultiHopQA）采样4603个问题，通过MCTS+SPRE生成13,289对高质量过程偏好样本。这些样本覆盖三类关键行为：

- 查询生成（Query Generation）
- 证据提取（Evidence Extraction）
- 答案生成（Answer Generation）

如上图 ... ，RAG-ProGuide覆盖了 ... 与多跳任务场景 ... 对，并反映了Agentic ... AG系统在动态决策过程中的 ... 关键子任务。
...
在拥有RAG-ProGuide数据集之后，ReasonRAG使用Direct Preference Optimization（DPO）进行过程级别的策略优化。
...
ReasonRAG通过设计合理的**推理控制流（Inference Pipeline）**实现了模型的自主决策。整个流程以模块化方式进行，模型可动态在多个状态之间跳转，并在必要时调用外部检索器以辅助生成答案。

模型从初始状态开始，最多进行𝑁轮推理。在每一轮中，模型依据当前状态调用策略函数决定接下来的动作：

- 如果处于 Reasoning 状态，模型需判断是否继续生成查询或答案，通过或进行标识。如果生成答案则进入Terminal状态，生成query则调用检索器并进入Grounding状态；

SOTA方法进行了系统 ... ，结果展示了Reason

- 数据效率高：仅用5k训练样本，ReasonRAG即在平均EM（34.4%）和F1（42.3%）上超越Search-R1（训练数据90k，EM 32.8%，F1 40.7%）。过程奖励显著优于传统的结果奖励。
- 多跳推理更强：在HotpotQA上，ReasonRAG以48.9%的F1分数超越AutoRAG（43.7%）和Search-R1（47.0%），展现出强大的复杂推理整合能力。

Subquadratic is the only company exclusively preoccupied with how foundation model algorithms scale with regards to compute, memory, and data. Most recent AI progress has come from scaling transformers with more parameters, data, and compute. We work on the scaling relationships underneath, with the goal of building most compute, memory, and sample efficient algorithms and models. We started with the attention, whose compute cost grows quadratically with context length in a standard transformer. To address this challenge, earlier this year we announced Subquadratic Sparse Attention (SSA), the architectural innovation that powers SubQ, the first fully subquadratic LLM, which has remained frontier-competitive through its updates.

Today we're releasing SubQ Snap, a decision model for agentic workflows built on the same foundational research. Our decision model is built to take the data-intensive but structured decisions inside an agentic workflow, like choosing which files are relevant, which tool to use next, whether a test result passes, or which step needs a frontier model. An agent makes these calls at nearly every turn, so a model that makes them quickly and correctly lowers the cost and latency of the whole workflow.
...

Powered by SSA, Snap is designed to process this growing context efficiently, without sacrificing the speed and accuracy that make a decision model useful in the first place. Thus, recent releases of decision models implement specialization in different ways. Laya, Perplexity's Decider, and TypeSafe's Jev expose the same interface (a question, a finite set of admissible answers, a structured prediction) but do so with differing architectural designs. Saluki 27B: Conway Research Compresses Qwen3.8-27B to Under 8 GB With 96% Benchmark Retention · GPTS24
...
Conway Research released Saluki 27B 1.0 on October 9, compressing Alibaba's 54-gigabyte Qwen3.8-27B to a 7.89-gigabyte GGUF file — a 6.84-fold reduction that the company says preserves 96% of the base model's benchmark performance across nine evaluations. The release arrives four days after Conway Research launched its Underdog on-device AI assistant, positioning Saluki 27B as the open-source inference backbone for a commercial product strategy built around consumer hardware.

At 7.89 gigabytes, Saluki 27B fits an 8-gigabyte-VRAM graphics card — an RTX 4060, an Arc A770 — and the base Apple M-series configuration. The Q4_K_M quantization of the same model requires roughly 17.1 gigabytes, demanding a 24-gigabyte GPU or higher-end Apple Silicon. Saluki 27B is the first quantization of Qwen3.8-27B accessible to the hardware class most developers own.
...
The explanation for Saluki's claimed retention is importance-matrix (imatrix) calibration — a technique in the llama.cpp ecosystem that runs a calibration dataset through the model before quantization to identify which weights most affect output quality, then rounds those positions more carefully. The released filename, `Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0-IQ2-mix.gguf`, confirms the IQ2-mix format from the IQ2 family; the specific calibration dataset used remains undisclosed. IQ2-family GGUF formats using imatrix consistently outperform naive Q2 quantization.
...
The most striking claim is not quality preservation but quality improvement on certain tasks. Conway Research reports Saluki 27B scores 88 on its Underdog Bench tool-calling evaluation against 84 for full-precision Qwen3.8-27B, and 42 versus 35 on parallel tool calls. A 2-bit quantization outperforming the base model on any benchmark is counterintuitive and warrants scrutiny.

Underdog Bench is a proprietary evaluation developed and run by Conway Research. Its methodology is not publicly documented and no independent team has reproduced its results. Imatrix calibration against tool-calling-heavy data could systematically improve performance on Underdog Bench's task distribution while degrading performance elsewhere. The independently validated failure mode is the one Conway Research discloses: AIME 2025 and 2026 scores fall by 15 to 18 points — a meaningful regression on benchmarks that test multi-step symbolic reasoning, where weight precision is known to matter most.
...
Before this release, the best option for an 8-gigabyte GPU was a Q4_K_M of a 7-to-9-billion-parameter model — a Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, or Gemma 2 9B, each 4-to-6 gigabytes. Saluki 27B reaches 27 billion parameters at a comparable file size, offering meaningfully greater depth for instruction-following and tool-use tasks — provided they do not depend on peak mathematical reasoning.
...
Saluki 27B is released under the Apache 2.0 license and runs on standard llama.cpp. Any developer can use it with Ollama, LM Studio, or a bare llama.cpp install. That openness is commercially deliberate.

Conway Research launched Underdog four days earlier, on October 5–6. The app runs via the company's proprietary Husky inference engine, optimized for Apple Silicon and separate from llama.cpp. Open-sourcing the Saluki GGUF weights under Apache 2.0 drives adoption across the llama.cpp ecosystem — Ollama, LM Studio, developer testing — while Conway Research keeps its inference advantage proprietary. Conway Research closed its funding round on October 2, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, and Anthology Fund; angel investors include Patrick Collison and Guillermo Rauch. The sequencing — capital close, Underdog launch, open GGUF release — is a coordinated go-to-market, not incidental research generosity.
...
Qwen3.8-27B was released August 14; Saluki 27B followed within eight weeks. Two facts are solid: the 7.89-gigabyte size unlocks 8-gigabyte hardware for a 27B model, and the AIME regression confirms math-heavy reasoning takes a real hit at 2-bit. Everything between those — the 96% aggregate retention, the tool-calling gains, the nine-benchmark summary — is company-reported data from a proprietary evaluation framework. When independent benchmarks arrive, they will determine whether Saluki's retention claim reflects a genuine step in 2-bit quantization quality or favorable benchmark selection — a result worth waiting for before committing Saluki to production workflows that depend on precision reasoning.

candidates.why_now: NVIDIA research on ReplaySSM shows significant speedups for SSM decoding and speculative decoding, addressing critical inference bottlenecks.

candidates.angle: True AI compute costs should be measured by useful AI work delivered per watt and dollar, not just raw GPU specs or rental rates.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers and companies struggle to assess the real economic efficiency of AI infrastructure based on traditional metrics.
candidates.why_now: Tensor Machines launched an open-source benchmark to link hardware performance, power, and AI output, offering a new standard.

candidates.audience_pain: Scaling AI infrastructure faces bottlenecks beyond just compute, requiring open standards and advanced system designs.
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA announced Vera Rubin's architecture and partnerships at OCP Global Summit, showcasing its role in next-gen AI infrastructure deployments.
candidates.hook_seed: NVIDIA Vera Rubin: scaling AI to gigawatts.
